# Why Jǫrð belongs in your address bar

Every address bar is a choice. When you type **Jǫrð**, you are not typing a novelty; you are restoring a name that the early DNS, built for English typewriters, could not carry. The plain ASCII form *jord* is a leftover of that constraint, not the name itself. This post is the long version of the restoration: where the name comes from, how the Runes tradition wrote it, how it is pronounced, what the myths and the material record preserve, and why its Unicode form now lives as a working domain. The claim throughout is simple — the original spelling is not decoration. It is the name.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Jǫrð
- **ASCII form:** jord
- **Meaning:** "Earth"
- **Domain of influence:** Earth, Mother of Thor
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Live domain:** jord.com

## Overview

**Jǫrð** (*jord*) — Earth, Mother of Thor · Earth — belongs to the Norse tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Earth, Mother of Thor". The name means "Earth".

**Jǫrð** belongs to the Norse tradition, where it is associated with earth, mother of thor.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Jǫrð** and serves its temple at [jord.com](https://punicodex.com/jord/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *jord* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Jǫrð** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Earth".

The reconstructed proto-form is *erþō* (proto-germanic, "earth"). Old Norse Jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō 'earth'; personified as a jötunn and mother of Thor by Odin.

The ASCII form *jord* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Jǫrð** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **j** → **J** — Same, capitalized
- **o** → **ǫ** — O with ogonek: nasalized vowel
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **d** → **ð** — Eth: voiced dental fricative

The canonical temple for this name is served at **jord.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Old Norse Jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō 'earth'; personified as a jötunn and mother of Thor by Odin.

The reconstructed proto-form is **erþō* (proto-germanic), glossed as "earth".

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The original script for this norse name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.

The form **Jǫrð** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/jord/** — Norse Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **J** — Initial character of the restored form Jǫrð.
- **ǫrð** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Norse tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'JORD' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Norse** — Jǫrð, the restored Unicode form of the name

Jǫrð is Tier 1 because the Norse form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

## Mythology

The stories of **Jǫrð** circulate within the Norse corpus, where the figure embodies earth, mother of thor.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Jǫrð is attested in the canonical Norse sources as a figure associated with earth, mother of thor.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Earth" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Jǫrð** is the personified earth in Norse myth and the mother of Thor by Odin. Her name is cognate with English "earth," and she represents the fertile ground that receives the sky's rain. Though little is said of her directly, her maternal bond to Thor makes her one of the most consequential figures in the pantheon. Snorri's *Gylfaginning* calls her one of Óðinn's wives and a daughter of Nótt and Annarr, linking her to the generative night and the primordial giantess line.

## The Unicode Restoration

Jǫrð is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *jord* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 4 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 2 further adjustments (ǫ, ð). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **jord.com**. Behind the scenes the DNS carries it in punycode form — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Jǫrð; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Runes can now be typed into any browser on earth.

Restoring **Jǫrð** is part of a larger effort to make the web multilingual by default. The PuniCodex project does not ask users to learn a new alphabet; it asks the infrastructure to respect the alphabets that already exist. Every section of this post — the script, the sound, the myths, the evidence — converges on the same point: the marks in Jǫrð are information, and information deserves an address of its own. A single Unicode domain is a small proof, but it is a proof that scales: every name restored makes the next one easier, and every visit to jord.com is a vote for the restored form.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Jǫrð**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *jord* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 4 characters, 2 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **j** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **o** becomes **ǫ** — O with ogonek: nasalized vowel.

The **r** stays as it is — Same.

The **d** becomes **ð** — Eth: voiced dental fricative.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

**Jǫrð** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Norse tradition, where it is counted among 95 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Jǫrð**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Jǫrð** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Jǫrð** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *jord*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.
